entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To be missed or neglected by a system, organization or group that should have noticed it or taken care of it.
entries.usage: Common in news and in talk about healthcare, schools and offices, about people or tasks that nobody takes responsibility for. The subject is the person or thing that gets missed: *kids who fall through the cracks*. At work it is a soft, blameless way to admit a mistake: *Sorry, your email fell through the cracks.*
entries.pattern: fall / slip through the cracks (of + system)
examples: Without a case manager, many homeless veterans **fall through the cracks** and never get the benefits they're owed.
Sorry for the late reply — your email **fell through the cracks** while I was traveling.
Mrs. Lopez checks in with every quiet kid so that nobody **falls through the cracks** in her crowded classroom.

drill.sentence: When Grandma switched pharmacies, her heart medication refill {{fell through the cracks}}, and nobody noticed for two weeks.
drill.hint: got missed by a system that should have caught it (not *slipped …*)

entries.related: *slip through the cracks* — same meaning; *fall through the net* — the British version; *get lost in the shuffle* — be forgotten during a busy or confusing time.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Postponed and not being worked on now because other things are more important, though it may be taken up again later.
entries.usage: Common at work and in personal plans, usually with *put* or *be*: *put a project on the back burner*. It sounds neutral and implies the plan is paused, not canceled, unlike *shelve* or *scrap*. The opposite, *on the front burner*, exists but is much less common.
entries.pattern: put something on the back burner / be on the back burner
examples: With the baby coming, we've put the kitchen remodel **on the back burner**.
The company put its electric truck program **on the back burner** after sales slowed.
My novel has been **on the back burner** for years, but I still write a page now and then.

drill.sentence: After the layoffs, Dana had to put her plans for grad school {{on the back burner}} and focus on paying rent.
drill.hint: aside as a low priority for now — a stove image

entries.related: *on hold* — paused, more neutral; *shelve* — postpone, often for a long or unknown time; *on ice* — informal, frozen for now.
entries.origin: From cooking on a stove: pots that only need to simmer are moved to the back burners while the front ones get attention.

entries.term: take something with a grain of salt
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To be somewhat skeptical about something you hear or read and not believe it completely.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation and online, often as advice: *Take it with a grain of salt.* It suggests the source may exaggerate or be biased, not that it is false. British English says *with a pinch of salt*, which Americans also understand.
entries.pattern: take something with a grain of salt
examples: My uncle claims he once caught a 200-pound tuna, but I **take** his fishing stories **with a grain of salt**.
Any poll this far before the election should be **taken with a grain of salt**.
The supplement company paid for its own study, so I'd **take that with a grain of salt**.

drill.sentence: My brother says the used car he's selling me is in perfect shape, but I'll {{take that with a grain of salt}} until a mechanic looks at it.
drill.hint: not fully believe it (the American version of the saying)

entries.related: *take something with a pinch of salt* — the British version; *be skeptical of* — plainer; *take something at face value* — the opposite, believe it as it appears.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To accept something exactly as it appears or is presented, without looking for a hidden meaning or questioning whether it is true.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, journalism and analysis, often in the negative as a warning: *don't take those numbers at face value*. In the positive, it can show deliberate trust: *I took her explanation at face value*. The object can be a statement, a number or a person: *I take people at face value*.
entries.pattern: take something / someone at face value
examples: When the seller swore the basement never flooded, we **took him at face value**. Big mistake.
The low unemployment rate shouldn't be **taken at face value**; many people have simply stopped looking for work.
She told me she was fine with the change, and I **took it at face value**. Only later did I realize she was hurt.

drill.sentence: The ad promised "unlimited data," and I was naive enough to {{take it at face value}} until my speed dropped after twenty gigabytes.
drill.hint: believe it as it appeared, without questioning it — a money image

entries.related: *take someone at their word* — believe what a person says; *read between the lines* — the opposite, look for the hidden meaning; *take something with a grain of salt* — doubt it a little.
entries.origin: From money: the *face value* of a coin, bill or stamp is the amount printed on it, which may differ from what it is really worth.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A collection of things, people or results that vary a lot in quality, some good and some bad.
entries.usage: A balanced, slightly disappointed verdict on reviews, results, seasons, collections or groups of people: *The reviews were a mixed bag.* It usually follows *be* and is often softened with *a bit of* or *something of*. It is milder than calling something bad and suggests there is no simple yes or no.
examples: The new album is **a mixed bag**: three great songs and a lot of filler.
The weather on our trip was **a bit of a mixed bag**, with two sunny days and four rainy ones.
Early results from the new bike lanes are **a mixed bag**; crashes are down, but some shop owners say they've lost customers.

drill.sentence: Dinner at the new Thai place was {{a mixed bag}}: the curry was amazing, but the noodles were cold and bland.
drill.hint: partly good, partly bad (not *hit or miss*)

entries.related: *hit or miss* — sometimes good, sometimes bad, about something done again and again; *a mixed blessing* — good overall but with disadvantages; *uneven* — plainer, about quality.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To manage to understand something that is complicated, strange or hard to accept.
entries.usage: Very common in American conversation, often in the negative or with *trying to* or *still*: *I can't wrap my head around it.* It works both for complex ideas and for shocking news that is hard to accept emotionally. *Get your head around* is the British equivalent, and *wrap your mind around* is also common.
entries.pattern: (can't / trying to) wrap your head around + something / how … / why …
examples: I still can't **wrap my head around** the fact that my little sister is getting married.
It took me a whole weekend to **wrap my head around** how attention works in language models.
Many homeowners are struggling to **wrap their heads around** the new property tax rules.

drill.sentence: I've read our mortgage paperwork three times, and I still can't {{wrap my head around}} how the interest is calculated.
drill.hint: fully understand — informal American phrase (not *make sense of*)

entries.related: *get your head around* — the British version; *make sense of* — neutral, fine in writing; *grasp* — more formal.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To become absorbed in a complicated or fascinating topic and spend far more time on it than you planned, often following one link or question after another.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation and online, usually about reading, research or the internet: *I went down a YouTube rabbit hole last night.* It is often humorous and self-mocking, or a mild warning about wasting time. A noun often goes before *rabbit hole*: *a Wikipedia rabbit hole*, *a conspiracy rabbit hole*.
entries.pattern: go / fall down a (+ noun) rabbit hole
examples: I looked up one fact about the Titanic and **went down a rabbit hole** until two in the morning.
Don't let the new hire **go down a rabbit hole** optimizing code that runs once a month.
After her diagnosis, my mom **went down a rabbit hole** of health forums and scared herself.

drill.sentence: I only meant to check the score, but I {{went down a rabbit hole}} of old highlight videos and lost the whole evening.
drill.hint: got absorbed for much longer than planned (not *fell …*)

entries.related: *fall down a rabbit hole* — same; *get sidetracked* — be distracted from your main task; *lose track of time* — not notice how much time has passed.
entries.origin: From *Alice's Adventures in Wonderland* (1865), in which Alice follows the White Rabbit down a hole into a strange world.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To hide a problem, mistake or scandal and avoid dealing with it, hoping nobody will notice.
entries.usage: Critical, used about institutions, families or leaders that cover up problems. The object usually goes in the middle (*sweep the complaints under the rug*), and the passive is common: *The issue was swept under the rug.* British English prefers *under the carpet*.
entries.pattern: sweep something under the rug / be swept under the rug
examples: For years, complaints about the director's temper were **swept under the rug**.
We can't just **sweep this under the rug**; the client will find the error eventually.
My parents never fought in front of us; every problem got **swept under the rug**.

drill.sentence: The coach knew about the hazing ritual but {{swept it under the rug}} to protect the team's winning season.
drill.hint: hid it instead of dealing with it — a housecleaning image (not *covered it up*)

entries.related: *cover up* — hide wrongdoing, stronger and more deliberate; *sweep under the carpet* — the British version; *bury your head in the sand* — ignore a problem rather than hide it.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To see how separate pieces of information are related and put them together to understand the whole situation.
entries.usage: Common in journalism, investigations and everyday reasoning. It often describes a failure (*nobody connected the dots*) or invites someone to reach an obvious conclusion: *You can connect the dots.* It can take *between A and B*, and British English says *join the dots*.
entries.pattern: connect the dots (between A and B)
examples: The warning signs were all there, but no agency **connected the dots** in time.
My mom noticed I was tired, quiet and skipping meals, and she **connected the dots** before I said a word.
A good doctor **connects the dots** between symptoms that seem unrelated.

drill.sentence: He'd been leaving work early and hiding his phone; it didn't take long for his wife to {{connect the dots}}.
drill.hint: see how the clues fit together (not *put two and two together*)

entries.related: *put two and two together* — work out the obvious truth from what you know; *join the dots* — the British version; *piece together* — gradually build the full picture.
entries.origin: From the children's puzzle in which you draw lines between numbered dots to reveal a picture.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Said to stress that something is not difficult to understand or to do.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and at work. It can reassure a nervous beginner, but it often sounds impatient or critical when someone has failed at something simple: *Come on, it's not rocket science.* Variants include *It's not brain surgery* and *You don't have to be a rocket scientist to …*
examples: Making bread at home **isn't rocket science**; you just need patience.
Pay people fairly and they'll stay longer — **it's not rocket science**.
Look, **it's not rocket science**: wash your hands and stay home when you're sick.

drill.sentence: Just water the plants twice a week and keep them out of direct sun. {{It's not rocket science}}.
drill.hint: this is easy — a spaceflight image (not *brain surgery*)

entries.related: *it's not brain surgery* — same; *a no-brainer* — an obvious choice; *a piece of cake* — very easy to do.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: An event or remark that makes someone see the real situation, especially after they have been too optimistic.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, sports and business, often with *need*, *get* or *give someone*: *the loss was a reality check for the team*. Telling someone *You need a reality check* is blunt and critical; *Let's do a quick reality check* sounds softer and suggests checking a plan together.
examples: Losing to a team from a much smaller school was **a reality check** for our players.
Paying my own rent for the first time gave me **a reality check** about how expensive life is.
Before we promise the client a June launch, we need **a reality check**: we're already two weeks behind.

drill.sentence: Mark thought he could run a marathon without training; cramping up at mile ten was {{a reality check}}.
drill.hint: a moment that showed him how things really are (not *a wake-up call* or *a rude awakening*)

entries.related: *a wake-up call* — an event that warns you to change something; *a dose of reality* — similar; *a rude awakening* — a sudden, unpleasant discovery of the truth.

entries.term: have a lot on your plate
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To have many tasks, responsibilities or problems to deal with at the same time.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation and workplace email, often to show sympathy or as a polite reason to say no: *I know you have a lot on your plate.* *Have got* also works, and the amount varies: *enough on my plate*, *too much on her plate*. It sounds friendly and understanding, not like a complaint.
entries.pattern: have (got) a lot / enough / too much on your plate
examples: I'd love to help with the fundraiser, but I **have a lot on my plate** right now.
With a new baby and a sick father, Jen **has a lot on her plate** this year.
I know you **have a lot on your plate**, so I'll keep this email short.

drill.sentence: Between finals, a part-time job and moving apartments, Luis {{has a lot on his plate}} this month.
drill.hint: is handling many responsibilities at once — a dinner image

entries.related: *have your hands full* — be very busy, often with people or children; *be swamped* — have too much work; *be stretched thin* — have too many demands on your time or resources.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To do much more than what is required or expected, usually to help someone.
entries.usage: Common in praise, thank-you notes, online reviews and performance evaluations: *She went above and beyond for our family.* It is often followed by *for* + person or *to* + verb, and *above and beyond the call of duty* is the fuller, more formal version. Saying it about yourself can sound like bragging.
entries.pattern: go above and beyond (for someone / to do something)
examples: The hotel staff **went above and beyond**, even driving us to the airport when our taxi didn't show up.
Our son's teacher **went above and beyond** to help him catch up after his surgery.
In her performance review, I wrote that Priya consistently **goes above and beyond** for her clients.

drill.sentence: The nurse {{went above and beyond}}, staying after her shift to make sure my father understood his new medications.
drill.hint: did far more than her job required (not *the extra mile*)

entries.related: *go the extra mile* — make more effort than needed, very similar; *above and beyond the call of duty* — fuller and more formal; *do the bare minimum* — the opposite.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To act in a way that permanently damages a relationship, so that you cannot go back to that person or place later.
entries.usage: Common in career and life advice, usually as a warning in the negative: *Don't burn your bridges.* It is typical when people talk about quitting a job, ending a partnership or leaving on bad terms. Both *burn bridges* and *burn your bridges* are common, and *with* names the other side.
entries.pattern: burn (your) bridges (with someone)
examples: Even if you hate your boss, don't **burn bridges** on your way out.
He **burned his bridges** with the whole family when he skipped his mother's funeral.
The chef **burned bridges** all over town by trashing his old restaurants in interviews.

drill.sentence: I'd love to tell my landlord exactly what I think of him, but I might need a reference someday, so I won't {{burn any bridges}}.
drill.hint: do anything that ruins the relationship for good

entries.related: *cut ties* — end a relationship, not always on bad terms; *mend fences* — repair a damaged relationship; *leave on good terms* — the opposite.
entries.origin: From armies that burned the bridges behind them, which made retreat impossible.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To decide which disagreements are important enough to fight about and let the less important ones go.
entries.usage: Very common advice for parents, couples and managers: *You have to pick your battles.* It sounds wise and practical, not weak. *Choose your battles* means the same, and the idea also appears as *That's not a battle worth fighting.*
examples: With a three-year-old, you learn to **pick your battles**; if she wants to wear rain boots in July, fine.
My manager told me to **pick my battles** and save my objections for things that really matter.
Roommates who don't **pick their battles** end up arguing about every dirty dish.

drill.sentence: Your teenager's messy room isn't worth a fight every night; you need to {{pick your battles}}.
drill.hint: decide which fights really matter (not *choose …*)

entries.related: *choose your battles* — same; *let it go* — stop worrying or arguing about something; *a hill to die on* — an issue you'll fight for at any cost.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A long and difficult struggle against strong opposition or many problems, in which success is uncertain.
entries.usage: Common in news, politics, sports and personal talk, usually with *face*, *fight* or *be*: *It's an uphill battle.* It stresses that the effort is hard and the result uncertain, not that it is hopeless. *An uphill struggle* and *an uphill fight* are common variants.
examples: Without a big label behind them, indie bands face **an uphill battle** to get on the radio.
Getting my dad to eat vegetables has always been **an uphill battle**.
Small bookstores are fighting **an uphill battle** against online retailers.

drill.sentence: After the injury, learning to walk again was {{an uphill battle}}, but she was back on the tennis court within a year.
drill.hint: a long, hard effort against the odds (not *… struggle*)

entries.related: *an uphill struggle* — same; *a losing battle* — a fight you cannot win; *a tall order* — a task or request that is very hard to meet.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Not yet decided or settled, so the outcome is still uncertain.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, work and news about plans, dates and decisions. It follows *be*, *remain* or *leave*, often with *still*: *Our plans are still up in the air.* It is neutral and often explains why you can't commit to something yet.
examples: Our summer vacation plans are still **up in the air** because of my husband's work schedule.
With the budget vote delayed, funding for the new library remains **up in the air**.
I can't sign the lease yet; everything's **up in the air** until I hear about the job.

drill.sentence: We know the wedding will be in the fall, but the exact date is still {{up in the air}}.
drill.hint: not decided yet — an idiom (not *undecided*)

entries.related: *in limbo* — stuck in an uncertain state, often for a long time; *up for grabs* — available for anyone to win; *TBD* — short for *to be determined*, in writing.

entries.term: err on the side of caution
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To choose the safer or more careful option when you are not sure what is right, even if it may turn out to be unnecessary.
entries.usage: Common in health, safety, legal and work contexts, and as a polite explanation of a cautious decision: *we decided to err on the side of caution*. The frame also works with other nouns: *err on the side of generosity*. *Err* rhymes with *air* or with *her*; both are standard in American English.
entries.pattern: err on the side of caution / of + noun
examples: The doctor said it was probably just a cold, but she **erred on the side of caution** and ordered a flu test.
With a big storm in the forecast, the school district **erred on the side of caution** and closed for the day.
If you're not sure how formal the dinner is, **err on the side of caution** and wear a jacket.

drill.sentence: The milk smelled fine, but it was a week past its date, so I {{erred on the side of caution}} and poured it out.
drill.hint: chose the safer option (not *played it safe*)

entries.related: *play it safe* — informal, avoid risk; *better safe than sorry* — a saying that gives the same advice; *take no chances* — be extremely careful.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To find out carefully how people will react to an idea or plan before you fully commit to it.
entries.usage: Common in business, politics, dating and career talk. It is used alone or with *by* + -ing: *She's testing the waters by sending out a few résumés.* The singular *test the water* is more common in British English.
examples: The author **tested the waters** with a short story before writing a whole novel set in that world.
We're opening a pop-up shop first to **test the waters** before signing a long lease.
She **tested the waters** by mentioning a dog in passing, to see how her husband would react.

drill.sentence: Before quitting his job to bake full-time, Sam {{tested the waters}} by selling bread at the Saturday farmers market.
drill.hint: checked people's reaction before fully committing (not *dipped a toe in*)

entries.related: *dip a toe in the water* — try something in a small, cautious way; *put out feelers* — quietly ask around to see what people think; *a trial balloon* — an idea floated to test public reaction.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Something that is hard to persuade people to accept, approve or buy.
entries.usage: Common in business, politics and everyday talk about ideas, plans and products: *a tax increase will be a tough sell*. It often takes *to* or *for* + the audience: *a tough sell to voters*. *A hard sell* can mean the same, but it also means an aggressive way of selling, so *a tough sell* is clearer.
entries.pattern: a tough sell (to / for + audience)
examples: A four-day workweek is **a tough sell** to the board, even if productivity goes up.
Camping in the rain was **a tough sell** for the kids, so we rented a cabin instead.
Raising bus fares is **a tough sell** in a city where many riders can barely afford them.

drill.sentence: My idea of a week at the lake with no phones was {{a tough sell}} to my teenagers.
drill.hint: something difficult to get people to accept (not *hard …*)

entries.related: *a hard sell* — same meaning, but also an aggressive sales style; *an easy sell* — the opposite; *a tall order* — a demand that is hard to meet.

entries.term: get your foot in the door
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To get a first, often small opportunity to enter an organization, industry or field, which can lead to better chances later.
entries.usage: Common in career advice and in talk about jobs, sales and show business: *An internship is a good way to get your foot in the door.* It suggests accepting a modest start to reach something bigger. *A foot in the door* also works with *have* or *give*: *The job gave her a foot in the door.*
entries.pattern: get your / a foot in the door (at / with + organization)
examples: She took an unpaid internship just to **get her foot in the door** at a fashion magazine.
The startup offered the first year free to **get its foot in the door** with big hospitals.
Lots of actors take tiny roles in commercials just to **get a foot in the door** in Hollywood.

drill.sentence: Working the front desk isn't glamorous, but it's a way to {{get your foot in the door}} at a big hotel chain.
drill.hint: get a first chance to enter the company (with *your*)

entries.related: *break into* — succeed in entering a field, as in *break into acting*; *get a break* — get a lucky opportunity; *start at the bottom* — begin in the lowest position.
entries.origin: From door-to-door salesmen, who put a foot in the doorway so the customer could not close the door.

entries.term: leave a lot to be desired
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To be much worse than it should be; to be clearly unsatisfactory.
entries.usage: A polite, understated way to criticize service, quality, skills or conditions, common in reviews, reports and conversation. The subject is the thing being judged: *The service left a lot to be desired.* *Leave much to be desired* is more formal, and *leave something to be desired* is milder.
examples: The food was fine, but the service **left a lot to be desired**.
Residents say the city's response to the flooding **left a lot to be desired**.
My cooking skills **leave a lot to be desired**, so we order takeout most nights.

drill.sentence: The hotel looked great online, but the cleanliness of the rooms {{left a lot to be desired}}.
drill.hint: was far below what it should have been (not *… much …*)

entries.related: *leave much to be desired* — more formal; *not up to par* — below the normal standard; *fall short* — fail to meet a standard.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To get ready to work hard on a practical or difficult task, and start doing it.
entries.usage: Common in speeches, at work and in everyday life, often as encouragement: *Let's roll up our sleeves and get to work.* It praises hands-on effort, as opposed to talk or planning. Politicians and managers like it because it makes them sound practical.
entries.pattern: roll up your sleeves (and + verb)
examples: The house needed a lot of work, so we **rolled up our sleeves** and started with the kitchen.
If we want this park cleaned up, we'll have to **roll up our sleeves** ourselves.
The new CEO promised to **roll up her sleeves** and fix the company's broken supply chain.

drill.sentence: Complaining about the messy garage won't fix it. It's time to {{roll up our sleeves}} and start sorting boxes.
drill.hint: get ready to work hard — a clothing image (with *our*)

entries.related: *get your hands dirty* — do practical, sometimes unpleasant work yourself; *buckle down* — start working seriously; *dig in* — start working or eating with energy.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To be deliberately slow in doing something, usually because you do not want to do it.
entries.usage: Critical, used about people, companies and governments that delay a decision or task. It is often in the progressive and often takes *on* + the task: *The landlord is dragging his feet on the repairs.* It suggests reluctance, not just slowness or laziness.
entries.pattern: drag your feet (on something)
examples: My son has been **dragging his feet** on his college applications all fall.
Critics say the state **dragged its feet** on testing the water after residents complained.
I know I'm **dragging my feet**, but I really don't want to start my taxes.

drill.sentence: The insurance company keeps {{dragging its feet}} on paying our claim, hoping we'll give up.
drill.hint: deliberately delaying (not *stalling*)

entries.related: *stall* — delay on purpose, often to gain time; *procrastinate* — put things off, often out of habit; *drag something out* — make something last longer than needed.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To do or say something, usually by accident or through carelessness, that damages your own interests or plans.
entries.usage: Common in politics, business and personal advice, often critical or as a warning: *You're only shooting yourself in the foot.* The reflexive pronoun matches the subject: *they shot themselves in the foot*. It stresses that the harm was self-inflicted and avoidable.
examples: Our players **shot themselves in the foot** with three silly penalties in the last two minutes.
If you skip breakfast before the exam, you're just **shooting yourself in the foot**.
The airline **shot itself in the foot** by cutting customer service right before the holidays.

drill.sentence: When she showed up forty minutes late to the job interview, Maya knew she had {{shot herself in the foot}}.
drill.hint: damaged her own chances — a gun image

entries.related: *score an own goal* — mainly British, harm your own side; *dig your own grave* — cause your own downfall; *backfire* — have the opposite effect to what was intended.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Said when you cannot do what you or someone else wants, because rules, orders or circumstances prevent you.
entries.usage: Common in customer service, management and official replies, often after *I'm sorry*: *I'd like to help, but my hands are tied.* It shifts responsibility to a rule or a higher authority, so it can sound like an excuse. The possessive changes with the subject: *their hands are tied*.
entries.pattern: someone's hands are tied (by + rule)
examples: I'd love to give you a refund, but **my hands are tied** — it's company policy.
The principal says **her hands are tied** because the dress code comes from the district.
My parents wanted to help with tuition, but with Dad out of work, **their hands were tied**.

drill.sentence: The referee knew the call felt unfair, but the rule was clear and {{his hands were tied}}.
drill.hint: he couldn't act freely — a body image

entries.related: *have no choice* — plainer; *be in a bind* — be in a difficult situation; *a free hand* — the opposite, the freedom to act as you like.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To blame or accuse someone, often publicly, for a problem or mistake.
entries.usage: Common in news, politics and arguments. The patterns are *point the finger at* someone and *point fingers* (blame each other): *Everyone's pointing fingers.* It is often critical of people who blame others instead of fixing the problem.
entries.pattern: point the finger at someone (for something)
examples: After the bridge collapsed, officials began **pointing the finger at** the construction company.
Before you **point the finger at** your brother, remember that you left the gate open too.
When the deal fell apart, the two companies **pointed fingers** at each other.

drill.sentence: When the car came back with a dent, my roommate immediately {{pointed the finger at}} his girlfriend.
drill.hint: accused — a hand-gesture image

entries.related: *play the blame game* — keep blaming others instead of solving the problem; *throw someone under the bus* — blame someone to save yourself; *take the blame* — accept responsibility.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A warning sign that something may be wrong or dangerous and needs attention.
entries.usage: Very common in talk about dating, money, hiring and health: *That's a huge red flag.* Typical patterns are *a big red flag*, *raise red flags* and *see red flags*. Online, the opposite *green flag* is now popular for a good sign in a person.
entries.pattern: a (big / huge) red flag; raise red flags
examples: A landlord who wants cash only and won't show you the apartment? That's **a red flag**.
Sudden weight loss without trying can be **a red flag** for a serious illness.
Investors ignored several **red flags** before the crypto exchange collapsed.

drill.sentence: He got angry every time I had dinner with my friends without him. Looking back, that was {{a red flag}}.
drill.hint: a sign that something was wrong (not *a warning sign*)

entries.related: *a warning sign* — plainer; *a green flag* — informal, a good sign, especially in a partner; *set off alarm bells* — make people worried that something is wrong.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To cause surprise or mild disapproval, usually because something is unusual or seems slightly improper.
entries.usage: Common in news and conversation about decisions, clothes, spending or behavior: *The choice raised eyebrows.* It is milder than *cause outrage* and is often used with *a few* or *some*. The adjective *eyebrow-raising* is also common.
entries.pattern: raise (a few / some) eyebrows
examples: Her bright red wedding dress **raised a few eyebrows** among the older guests.
The museum's decision to hire the director's nephew **raised eyebrows** among the staff.
Paying twelve dollars for a cup of coffee will **raise eyebrows** even in New York.

drill.sentence: When our quiet accountant showed up to the holiday party with blue hair, it {{raised a few eyebrows}}.
drill.hint: caused some surprise and mild disapproval (not *turned heads*)

entries.related: *turn heads* — attract attention, often admiring; *cause a stir* — create excitement or concern; *ruffle feathers* — annoy or upset people.

entries.term: bury your head in the sand
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To ignore an unpleasant problem or fact and refuse to deal with it, hoping it will go away.
entries.usage: Critical, used in news, politics and personal advice about debt, health or climate: *We can't keep burying our heads in the sand.* The possessive matches the subject, and plural subjects take *heads*. It describes ignoring a problem yourself, not hiding it from others.
examples: You can't **bury your head in the sand** forever; that noise in the engine isn't going away.
Coastal cities can't keep **burying their heads in the sand** about rising sea levels.
My dad **buried his head in the sand** about his chest pains until he ended up in the ER.

drill.sentence: Instead of opening his credit card bills, Kevin just {{buries his head in the sand}} and hopes they'll disappear.
drill.hint: refuses to face the problem — an ostrich image

entries.related: *turn a blind eye* — deliberately ignore something wrong, often someone else's behavior; *in denial* — refusing to accept the truth; *sweep something under the rug* — hide a problem from others.
entries.origin: From the popular belief that ostriches hide their heads in the sand when in danger, which they do not actually do.

entries.term: get your ducks in a row
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To get everything well organized and prepared before you start something.
entries.usage: Common in American work and everyday talk, especially about paperwork, plans and money. It is friendly and slightly humorous. Common forms are *have your ducks in a row* and *get all your ducks in a row*.
examples: Before you meet with the tax accountant, **get your ducks in a row**: receipts, forms, everything.
The two companies wanted to **get their ducks in a row** before announcing the merger.
Once we **got our ducks in a row**, the mortgage approval took just two weeks.

drill.sentence: Before the baby arrives, we want to {{get our ducks in a row}}: the crib, the car seat and the hospital bag.
drill.hint: get everything organized and ready — a bird image

entries.related: *get your act together* — start behaving in a more organized way, often critical; *get organized* — plainer; *have everything lined up* — have all arrangements ready.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To argue for the opposite view, even if you do not believe it, in order to test an idea or start a discussion.
entries.usage: Common in meetings, classes and friendly debate, usually announced in advance so it sounds less confrontational: *Let me play devil's advocate for a second.* It signals that you are challenging the idea, not the person. The noun also works alone: *She's always the devil's advocate.*
examples: Just to **play devil's advocate**, what if the cheaper option is actually good enough?
My philosophy professor loved to **play devil's advocate** and argue that free will doesn't exist.
I agree with you, but let me **play devil's advocate**: a lot of people can't afford to move.

drill.sentence: I actually like your plan for the camping trip, but I'll {{play devil's advocate}}: what if it rains all week?
drill.hint: argue the other side on purpose to test the idea

entries.related: *push back* — disagree with or resist an idea; *the other side of the coin* — the opposite aspect of a situation; *a contrarian* — a person who habitually takes the opposite view.
entries.origin: From the Catholic Church, where an official called the *devil's advocate* argued against making a person a saint.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To try to reach the same level as others after falling behind them.
entries.usage: Common in business, sports and school: *The company is playing catch-up with its rivals.* It often suggests you are behind because you started late or made a mistake. *Catch-up* is hyphenated here, and *with* or *on* often follows.
entries.pattern: play catch-up (with someone / on something)
examples: After missing two weeks with the flu, my son is **playing catch-up** in math.
Many older carmakers are still **playing catch-up** on electric vehicles.
The Giants gave up two early touchdowns and **played catch-up** for the rest of the game.

drill.sentence: Our town didn't build any new housing for twenty years, and now it's {{playing catch-up}} as rents soar.
drill.hint: struggling to reach a level others have already reached (not *trying to …*)

entries.related: *fall behind* — fail to keep up with others; *close the gap* — reduce the distance to others; *keep up* — stay at the same level.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Said when the chance to do something has passed and it is too late now.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and at work, usually as a short, resigned or humorous reply to an idea that comes too late. It often follows a regret or a suggestion: *We could have bought a house in 2015, but that ship has sailed.* *That ship sailed long ago* is also common.
examples: I once thought about becoming a doctor, but at fifty-two, **that ship has sailed**.
We should have booked the cheap flights in March, but **that ship has sailed**.
Asking for a smaller budget now? **That ship sailed** when the council voted last month.

drill.sentence: You want to apologize to Emma now? She's married and lives in Denver. I think {{that ship has sailed}}.
drill.hint: the chance is gone for good — a boat image

entries.related: *that train has left the station* — a process has already started and cannot be stopped; *miss the boat* — fail to take a chance in time; *too little, too late* — an action that comes too late to help.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Being strongly criticized or attacked, especially in public, for something you have done.
entries.usage: Very common in news headlines and reports about politicians, companies and officials: *The CEO is under fire over the layoffs.* It usually follows *be* or *come*, with *over* or *for* + the reason: *come under fire for* + -ing. The literal military sense (being shot at) also exists, so context matters.
entries.pattern: be / come under fire (over / for something)
examples: The school board is **under fire** for cutting music and art programs.
The airline **came under fire** after videos of passengers stuck on the runway for six hours went viral.
The referee was **under fire** from both teams' fans after the controversial penalty.

drill.sentence: The ticket company is {{under fire}} for adding huge hidden fees to concert tickets.
drill.hint: facing harsh public criticism (not *… attack* or *in hot water*)

entries.related: *in hot water* — in trouble, often for breaking a rule; *under scrutiny* — being examined closely; *take flak* — informal, receive criticism.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To stop a project, plan or activity, especially by ending the money or support it needs.
entries.usage: Common in business, media and politics: *The studio pulled the plug on the sequel.* The usual pattern is *pull the plug on* + the project. It sounds abrupt and final, and the subject is usually the person or organization with the power to fund or approve.
entries.pattern: pull the plug on something
examples: The network **pulled the plug** on the show after only six episodes.
The city **pulled the plug** on the new stadium when the cost estimate doubled.
We were planning a big wedding, but we **pulled the plug** on it and eloped instead.

drill.sentence: The school {{pulled the plug}} on the senior trip when only twelve students signed up.
drill.hint: put an end to it — an electrical image

entries.related: *call off* — cancel an event; *scrap* — get rid of a plan completely; *put on hold* — stop for now, not permanently.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: An immediate, automatic response to something, made without careful thought.
entries.usage: Usually critical, especially in politics, the media and management: *a knee-jerk reaction to bad news*. It is often followed by *to* + the event. *Knee-jerk* also works as an adjective on its own: *knee-jerk criticism*, *a knee-jerk response*.
entries.pattern: a knee-jerk reaction (to something)
examples: Banning all dogs from the park after one bite seems like **a knee-jerk reaction**.
My **knee-jerk reaction** was to say no, but I thought about the offer overnight and changed my mind.
Selling all your stocks after one bad week is **a knee-jerk reaction** most financial advisers warn against.

drill.sentence: When the vacuum cleaner broke, my {{knee-jerk reaction}} was to buy a new one, but a ten-dollar part fixed it.
drill.hint: instant, unthinking response — a reflex image (not *gut …*)

entries.related: *a gut reaction* — an instinctive feeling, often trusted rather than criticized; *jump to conclusions* — decide something too quickly without the facts; *a reflex* — an automatic response.
entries.origin: From the knee reflex a doctor tests by tapping just below the kneecap, which makes the leg kick automatically.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: While something is already happening, without stopping or preparing in advance.
entries.usage: Common at work and in everyday talk about improvising: *We'll have to figure it out on the fly.* It goes after the verb, typically *change*, *adjust*, *decide*, *learn* or *translate*. In computing it means *during processing, not beforehand*: *files compressed on the fly*.
examples: Our tour guide got sick, so I had to translate **on the fly** for the whole group.
The app resizes photos **on the fly**, so the page loads quickly on phones.
With twins, you learn to change your plans **on the fly**.

drill.sentence: The best man lost his notes, so he made up his toast {{on the fly}}, and it was the funniest speech of the night.
drill.hint: while already in progress, without preparing (not *on the spot* or *off the cuff*)

entries.related: *on the spot* — immediately, at that moment; *wing it* — improvise without preparation; *as you go* — during the process.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To force someone to answer a difficult question or make a decision immediately, often in front of other people.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and meetings, often in apologies or complaints: *Sorry to put you on the spot.* It suggests pressure and some embarrassment, especially in public. The person goes between *put* and *on*: *put me on the spot*.
entries.pattern: put someone on the spot
examples: I don't want to **put you on the spot**, but can you give us a rough cost estimate today?
My aunt **put me on the spot** at dinner by asking when I'm getting married.
The reporter **put the coach on the spot** with a question about his star player's contract.

drill.sentence: The teacher {{put him on the spot}} by asking him to explain the answer in front of the whole class.
drill.hint: pressured him to respond right away (not *embarrassed him*)

entries.related: *catch someone off guard* — surprise someone who isn't ready; *in the hot seat* — in a position where you must answer hard questions; *call someone out* — publicly criticize someone.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A remark that sounds like praise but actually contains an insult or criticism.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and in commentary on social behavior. Typical examples are *You look great for your age* and *You're smarter than you look*. The adjective also works alone: *That was a bit backhanded.*
examples: "You're so brave to wear that" is a classic **backhanded compliment**.
My mother-in-law said my cooking was "surprisingly edible" — **a backhanded compliment** at best.
The coach said I played "better than he expected," which felt like **a backhanded compliment**.

drill.sentence: When my friend said my new haircut made me look "much less tired," I realized it was {{a backhanded compliment}}.
drill.hint: praise that is really an insult (not *a dig*)

entries.related: *a dig* — informal, a small hidden insult; *damn with faint praise* — criticize by praising weakly; *a left-handed compliment* — an older variant.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Affecting everyone or everything in a group or organization equally.
entries.usage: Common in business, economics and news, especially about pay, prices, cuts and taxes. It can follow the verb (*Prices rose across the board*) or come before a noun with hyphens: *across-the-board tax cuts*. It stresses that no group is left out or treated differently.
entries.pattern: across the board / across-the-board + noun
examples: Prices at the grocery store have gone up **across the board**, from eggs to coffee.
The company announced **across-the-board** raises of three percent.
Our team improved **across the board** this season: better defense, better passing and fewer injuries.

drill.sentence: The school is cutting budgets {{across the board}}, so every department, from sports to science, will lose money.
drill.hint: for every part equally, with no exceptions (not *everywhere*)

entries.related: *blanket* — applying to all cases, as in *a blanket ban*; *wholesale* — complete and large-scale, often negative; *one-size-fits-all* — the same for everyone, usually a criticism.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: The best example of something, used as the standard against which similar things are judged.
entries.usage: Common in medicine, science, business and journalism: *Randomized trials are the gold standard.* It usually takes *of*, *for* or *in* + the field. In medicine it is close to a technical term for the best available test or treatment.
examples: That hotel is still **the gold standard** of customer service, decades after it opened.
A biopsy remains **the gold standard** for diagnosing most cancers.
Grandma's apple pie is **the gold standard** that every other pie in the family is judged against.

drill.sentence: For many puzzle fans, the Sunday crossword in The New York Times is {{the gold standard}}.
drill.hint: the best example that all others are measured against (not *the benchmark*)

entries.related: *the benchmark* — a point of comparison, not necessarily the best; *best in class* — business jargon for the best in a category; *second to none* — better than all others.
entries.origin: From the monetary system in which a country's currency was backed by a fixed amount of gold.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: More advanced or modern than others, or acting earlier than others in response to a trend or change.
entries.usage: Common in business, technology, fashion and policy talk, usually as praise: *The company stayed ahead of the curve on remote work.* It follows *be*, *stay* or *keep*, often with *on* + the trend. The opposite, *behind the curve*, is critical.
examples: My grandmother was **ahead of the curve**; she was composting long before it was trendy.
The city stayed **ahead of the curve** by installing electric car chargers ten years ago.
Investors who bought into solar early were well **ahead of the curve**.

drill.sentence: Our school was {{ahead of the curve}} on online classes, so the switch during the pandemic was easy.
drill.hint: earlier than others in following a trend (not *… of the game* or *… of its time*)

entries.related: *ahead of its time* — too modern to be appreciated in its own time; *ahead of the game* — well prepared, in a strong position; *behind the curve* — the opposite.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To set a higher standard for what is expected or for what others must achieve.
entries.usage: Common in business, sports, education and reviews, usually as praise: *This phone raises the bar for battery life.* It often takes *for* + the field or the people affected. The opposite, *lower the bar*, is critical and suggests that standards are being reduced.
entries.pattern: raise the bar (for + field / people)
examples: Her Olympic routine **raised the bar** for every gymnast who came after her.
That new place on Fifth Street has really **raised the bar** for pizza in our neighborhood.
The state is **raising the bar** for new teachers by requiring a longer training period.

drill.sentence: The new smartphone {{raises the bar}} for camera quality, so its competitors will have to catch up.
drill.hint: makes the expected standard higher — a high-jump image

entries.related: *set the bar high* — have high standards from the start; *up the ante* — increase the stakes or demands; *lower the bar* — the opposite.
entries.origin: From the high jump and pole vault, where the bar is raised after each round.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To fail to achieve the intended result or effect, or to be inaccurate.
entries.usage: Common in reviews, criticism and analysis: *The movie's jokes mostly miss the mark.* It is a polite, slightly formal way to say something failed or was wrong, often with *completely* or *badly*. The opposites are *hit the mark* and *be on the mark*.
examples: The ad was meant to be funny, but it **missed the mark** and offended a lot of viewers.
The forecasters **missed the mark** badly; we got a foot of snow instead of a light dusting.
My attempt at a surprise party **missed the mark** — my wife hates surprises.

drill.sentence: The movie tries hard to be both a comedy and a love story, but it {{misses the mark}} on both counts.
drill.hint: fails to achieve what it aims for — an archery image (not *falls short*)

entries.related: *fall short* — not reach a required level; *fall flat* — fail to amuse or impress; *wide of the mark* — inaccurate, more common in British English.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A situation in which you have to learn a lot of new things in a short time, which takes great effort.
entries.usage: Common at work and in talk about new jobs, tools, hobbies and life changes, with *have*, *face* or *come with*. On a real learning-curve graph, a steep curve means fast progress, but in everyday use *steep* means hard. Everyone understands it that way, so use it with confidence.
examples: Becoming a parent comes with **a steep learning curve**; nobody tells you how little you'll sleep.
The new accounting software has **a steep learning curve**, but it saves hours once you know it.
Moving to Japan without speaking Japanese meant **a steep learning curve** for the whole family.

drill.sentence: Sailing looks relaxing, but there's {{a steep learning curve}} in the first season: knots, wind, tides and a lot of falling in.
drill.hint: a lot to master in a short time — a graph image

entries.related: *be thrown in the deep end* — be given a hard task with no preparation; *get up to speed* — reach the knowledge level needed; *trial by fire* — learning under great pressure.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Involved in a situation that is too difficult for you to manage, because you lack the skill, knowledge or resources.
entries.usage: Common in conversation about jobs, debt, relationships and projects: *I'm in over my head.* It follows *be*, *get* or *feel*, and the possessive matches the subject. It is often an honest admission, but said about someone else it can sound critical or worried.
entries.pattern: be / get in over your head (with something)
examples: I offered to plan my best friend's wedding, and now I'm totally **in over my head**.
The new manager was clearly **in over his head** and quit after three months.
Many first-time buyers **got in over their heads** with adjustable-rate mortgages before 2008.

drill.sentence: When I offered to fix the bathroom pipes myself, I didn't realize how quickly I'd be {{in over my head}}.
drill.hint: facing something too difficult to handle (not *out of my depth*)

entries.related: *out of your depth* — very similar; *bite off more than you can chew* — take on more than you can handle; *swamped* — have too much to do, but not necessarily too hard.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To reduce or remove a difference or distance between two things, groups or ideas.
entries.usage: Common in news, policy, business and education, usually as *bridge the gap between A and B*. It can also mean covering a temporary shortage: *a loan to bridge the gap until payday*. It sounds positive and constructive.
entries.pattern: bridge the gap between A and B
examples: The program aims to **bridge the gap** between high school and college for first-generation students.
Our daughter **bridges the gap** between her grandparents, who only speak Spanish, and her dad, who only speaks English.
I took a part-time job to **bridge the gap** until my new position started in March.

drill.sentence: Our yearly block party has helped {{bridge the gap}} between longtime residents and newcomers.
drill.hint: connect two separated groups (not *close …*)

entries.related: *close the gap* — reduce a difference, especially in numbers or performance; *meet halfway* — compromise; *build bridges* — improve relations between groups.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: At some point in the future, often several months or years from now.
entries.usage: Common in American conversation, business and politics. It usually comes at the end of the clause, often with *a few years* or *somewhere*: *a few years down the road*. It can also mean literally farther along the street, so context matters.
examples: We're renting for now, but we'd like to buy a house **down the road**.
Skipping oil changes saves money today but costs a lot more **down the road**.
A few years **down the road**, nobody will remember this argument.

drill.sentence: Kids who learn to manage money early are less likely to struggle with debt {{down the road}}.
drill.hint: in the future — an image of a long drive

entries.related: *down the line* — same, common in British and American English; *in the long run* — over a long period, with a final result; *somewhere along the way* — at some point during a process.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A good or hopeful aspect of a bad or difficult situation.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, news and comforting talk: *The silver lining is that nobody was hurt.* Typical patterns are *the silver lining is that …* and *find a silver lining in* something. It can sound forced or insensitive if the situation is very serious.
entries.pattern: the silver lining is that … / a silver lining to something
examples: Losing my job was hard, but **the silver lining** was finally having time to finish my degree.
The **silver lining** of our canceled flight was an extra night in Rome.
If there's **a silver lining** to the drought, it's that people are finally taking water conservation seriously.

drill.sentence: The storm knocked out our power for three days, but {{the silver lining}} was that the kids played board games instead of watching screens.
drill.hint: the good part of a bad situation (not *the upside* or *the bright side*)

entries.related: *the bright side* — the positive part, as in *look on the bright side*; *a blessing in disguise* — something that seemed bad but turned out good; *the upside* — plainer.
entries.origin: From the proverb *Every cloud has a silver lining*, based on an image in John Milton's poem *Comus* (1634).
